common_name: Whale's Tongue Agave (Broad-Leaved Silvery Blue Agave)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil in full sun; Whale's Tongue Agave is notably more cold-hardy than many other agave species and forms a large, symmetrical rosette of broad, thick, powdery blue-gray leaves.

directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; agave requires perfect drainage and quickly rots in heavy clay or wet sites. Whale's Tongue Agave forms one of the boldest and most architectural rosettes among cold-hardy agave species, with wide, cupped, powdery blue-gray leaves that curve upward like a whale's tongue, giving strong sculptural presence in a xeric or Mediterranean-style garden. It is notably more cold-tolerant than many ornamental agave species, making it a good choice at the cooler edge of typical agave range, and it needs essentially no supplemental water once established beyond occasional deep soaking in extended drought. Like most agaves it is monocarpic, flowering once on a tall stalk after many years and then dying, though it may produce offsets (pups) before or after flowering that can be separated and replanted.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pixwell holds its berries away from the thorny stems on longer stalks, making harvest noticeably easier than many gooseberry cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in hot climates. Pixwell was bred specifically to make gooseberry picking less painful, holding its pale green, ripening-to-pink berries on longer stems that dangle clear of the thorny branches, unlike older cultivars whose fruit clusters tightly among the spines. The berries have the classic tart gooseberry flavor, excellent for pies, preserves, and sauces, and the plant is vigorous, cold-hardy, and self-fertile, needing no separate pollinator. Prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush productive, and site with some afternoon shade in warmer climates, since gooseberries generally prefer cooler growing conditions than the Deep South provides.

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Crandall is a clove currant selection notably more heat- and drought-tolerant than European black and red currants, making it one of the few currants that performs reasonably well in the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Crandall is a selection of clove currant, a North American native species distinct from and considerably more heat- and drought-tolerant than the European black and red currants that struggle in hot summers, making it one of the more workable currant options for warmer zones. In spring it produces abundant, intensely spice-clove-scented yellow flowers that perfume the surrounding garden before setting large, sweet-tart black currants used fresh or in preserves. It is generally self-fertile though yields improve with a second plant nearby, and needs only routine removal of the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the shrub vigorous and productive.

common_name: Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry (Brilliant Fall Color Multi-Season Native Tree)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Autumn Brilliance is prized for white spring flowers, edible summer berries, and outstanding orange-red fall color all on the same plant.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Autumn Brilliance is one of the most widely planted serviceberry cultivars for its exceptional multi-season interest: clouds of white flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge, sweet, blueberry-like edible fruit in early summer that birds also relish, and some of the most reliable, brilliant orange-red fall foliage color of any small flowering tree. It works well as a single or multi-trunked small specimen tree, a large shrub border, or a naturalized planting, and tolerates a range of soil conditions with minimal care once established. The berries can be harvested for fresh eating, baking, and preserves if picked before birds strip the tree, or left entirely for wildlife.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Regent is a compact shrub-form saskatoon serviceberry selected specifically for heavy production of sweet, juicy fruit on a size manageable for home gardens and hedgerows.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Regent is a compact selection of saskatoon serviceberry, bred specifically as a fruiting shrub rather than a landscape specimen tree, producing heavy crops of sweet, blueberry-like berries on a manageable-sized bush well suited to home orchards, hedgerows, and edible landscaping. It shares the white spring flowers and good fall color of its tree-form relatives but stays considerably smaller, making it easier to net against birds and to harvest by hand. It is self-fertile, cold-hardy, and low-maintenance, needing only occasional removal of the oldest stems to keep the planting vigorous and productive.
